In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This important resource paper describes a collection of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) produced from patients with a microdeletion of the 16p11.2 chromosomal locus, well-known to be associated with significant neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric abnormalities. The work provides both a cautionary tale about some unexpected consequences of the reprogramming process, as well as a plethora of information about changes in gene expression observed when neural progenitors are derived from these iPSCs. The results provided here, combined with the availability of these iPSCs from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative, should be useful to developmental neurobiologists, those interested in psychiatric disease, and, frankly, to anyone interested in large-scale iPSC-based disease modeling.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "16p11.2 CNV Imparts Transcriptional Alterations in Neural Development in an hiPSC Model of Corticogenesis" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to either limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary:

The authors produced 65 iPSC clones from 13 individuals with CNVs at the 16p11.2 locus – 10 with microdeletions and 3 with microduplications. This locus is well-known to be associated with neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric abnormalities. The donor cells were provided by the Simons Foundation who also will make the iPSC clones available, making this a valuable cellular resource for those interested in this chromosomal locus and its role in brain development and function. The authors carried out a detailed analysis of the iPSC clones, produced using episomal reprogramming vectors, finding that many of the clones were compromised by unexpected, random integration of the reprogramming vectors with consequent effects on gene transcription in derived cells. The production of this large set of iPSC clones, as well as the cautionary tale concerning vector integration and a detailed RNAseq analysis of the integration-free clones make this paper, as a Tools and Resource publication, a valuable resource for the community.

Revisions for this paper:

We are mindful that additional experiments cannot be readily done at the moment. However, we believe that addressing some of these points, together with a reanalysis of the current data, will make this paper more useful to those interested in this area:

1) The data in this paper are restricted to iPSCs generated by episomal reprogramming. Since many, perhaps most, investigators are using Sendai virus, the authors should mention that point. Also do they conclude that episomal reprogramming should be avoided?

2) The analysis uses each clone a separate entity. As best as the reviewers can judge, 6 affected donors, not all of whom were diagnosed with ASD, 3 of which had 3 clones, 1 of which had 2 and the other 2 had 1 each, were used. There were also 3 unaffected donors (with 3, 2, and 2 clones). However, clones should not be weighted the same as individual donors. From Hoffman et al. Nat Comm 2017: "Due to the "repeated measures" study design where individuals are represented by multiple independent hiPSC-NPC and hiPSC-neuron lines, we used a linear mixed model by applying the duplicateCorrelation function in our limma/voom analysis. This approach is widely used to control the false positive rate in studies of repeated measures and its importance in hiPSC data sets was recently emphasized (citing Germain and Testa SCR 2017)". We recommend that the authors reanalyze their data so that each entry is a patient-associated value, rather than a clone-associated one.

3) Based on the results shown in this paper, it is a bit misleading to "strongly suggest" that "16p11.2 deletion may impact many functions important to neurodevelopment and neuropsychiatric disease" – given that the transcriptional changes reported are quite limited and that no data of any observable phenotype was presented. It would be appropriate to tone down that statement and draw more conservative conclusions.

4) Unless the authors wish to include data for the duplication clones, The title "16p11.2 CNV imparts…" should be "16p11.2 microdeletion imparts…" since all duplication hiPSC clones in the analysis were excluded in the analysis steps of Figure 5 and 6.

5) QC questions:

a) Information on the controls is lacking in the main manuscript. Could the authors specifically clarify (in the Results or Materials and methods) the extent to which cases and controls are sex-, ethnicity- and age-matched, as well as whether they were reprogrammed together with the cases and by the same methods?

b) What was the polygenic risk score for the patients/controls? Might this have accounted for variable clinical presentations?

c) Were the hiPSCs karyotyped?

d) What QC was performed on RNAseq to confirm sample identity, cell type composition, etc? It would be helpful if the authors applied variance partition to uncover to what extent variation is explained by reprogramming method, genotype, donor, diagnosis, cell type, etc?

e) What is the Spearman's correlation coefficients for transcriptomic gene expression between donors and clones samples?

6) Questions involving additional useful data analysis

a) Integration with existing datasets and psychiatric genetic studies: Is there an enrichment of 16p11.2 DEGs for the GWAS loci for ASD, SZ or ADHD? Can the authors also test for enrichment of postmortem disease signatures as reported by the CommonMind Consortium, NIH HBCC and/or PsychEncode UCLA (Geschwind) analyses?

b) Are gene expression differences validated in existing 16p11.2 postmortem, hiPSC or mouse datasets (ie. PMID: 26829649)?

c) Given some recent discussions of convergence between CNV effects in psychiatric disease, are major findings from 16p11.2 conserved in hiPSC neuron datasets from other major CNVs (ie. 22q11.2 hiPSC PMID: 27846841 and mouse PMID: 29666363; 15q11.2 BioRxiv https://doi.org/10.1101/772541; NRXN1 PMID: 31784728)

d) Can the authors discuss whether they believe the genome-wide transcriptomic effects of 16p11.2 reflect chromatin loops between the CNV locus and other target genes? miR targets? Or downstream impacts of perturbed neuronal maturation/activity/signaling?

7) Are the authors able to comment on any phenotypic differences that they did observe between microdeletion lines and wt lines?

Revisions expected in follow-up work:

1) Characterization of micro-duplication lines.

2) Elaboration of phenotypic differences at the neural progenitor stage or in differentiated neurons.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that 16p11.2 CNVs are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders and reciprocal physiological phenotypes based on prior literature. These claims describe the known clinical landscape of 16p11.2 deletions and duplications, including associations with ASD, SCZ, macro/microcephaly, and BMI differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C18 and C96 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing the clinical phenotypes associated with 16p11.2 CNVs. These represent established knowledge in the field and provide appropriate context for the current study.

results.result: The authors generated 65 hiPSC clones from 13 donors with 16p11.2 CNVs (10 deletion, 3 duplication donors) and characterized the demographic and clinical features of the donor cohort. The cohort includes diverse ages (5-41 years), both sexes, and various clinical diagnoses including ASD, articulation disorder, and language disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C25-C26, and C36-C44 provide clear documentation of the hiPSC resource generated, including donor demographics and clinical phenotypes. The data are presented transparently with appropriate detail about the cohort composition.

results.result: The authors successfully reprogrammed fibroblasts using episomal vectors and validated hiPSC pluripotency through multiple quality control measures including immunofluorescence for pluripotency markers (>95% positive), tri-lineage differentiation capacity, SNP array confirmation of diploidy and donor identity, and verification of 16p11.2 CNV breakpoints.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C52 describe comprehensive quality control of the hiPSC lines with appropriate validation methods. The pluripotency markers, differentiation capacity, and genetic characterization provide strong evidence for successful reprogramming and line quality.

results.result: The authors differentiated hiPSCs into cortical neural progenitor cells using dual-SMAD inhibition, generating neural rosettes with appropriate radial glial characteristics including PAX6 expression, apical-basal polarity markers (NCAD, ZO-1, aPKCζ), and proper mitotic cell localization. All clones showed enrichment for anterior and dorsal cortical markers, and cells could be further differentiated to immature neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C61 demonstrate successful neural differentiation with appropriate characterization. Flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and RNA-seq data support the establishment of cortical neural progenitor identity across genotypes.

results.result: The authors discovered that many hiPSC clones contained cryptically integrated reprogramming vectors despite using 'non-integrating' episomal methods. Integration led to inappropriate expression of reprogramming genes (particularly OCT3/4) in NPCs, causing differential expression of >3600 genes and having a more penetrant effect on transcription than the 16p11.2 CNVs themselves. This led to exclusion of integration-positive clones from subsequent analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C74 provide compelling evidence for the impact of cryptic vector integration through PCA, pseudo-alignment analysis, qPCR validation, and differential expression analysis. The decision to exclude Int+ clones is well-justified given the magnitude of transcriptional effects (>3600 DE genes). The development of a novel bioinformatic pipeline to detect integration is a valuable methodological contribution.

results.result: In integration-free clones, the authors identified 107 differentially expressed genes between 16p11.2 deletion and wild-type NPCs, including 14 downregulated genes within the 16p11.2 locus (consistent with copy number effects) and 93 genes outside the deletion interval. The DE gene list is enriched for ASD-associated genes and shows strong concordance across individual deletion clones. An orthogonal analysis using limma/voom identified 40 DE genes with 17 overlapping with the primary analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C83 present robust differential expression analysis with appropriate batch correction (SVA), qPCR validation of key genes (KCTD13, TAOK2, MAPK3, SEZ6L2), and orthogonal validation using an alternative statistical approach. The consistency across individual clones and validation methods strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: The authors determined that only a subset of genes within the 16p11.2 locus are expressed in early NPCs (41 of 56 genes), with 14 showing significant downregulation in deletion clones. All 14 DE genes were located within the overlapping deletion interval across donors with known breakpoints.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 and C99-C103 provide clear characterization of which 16p11.2 genes are expressed and affected in early NPCs. The finding that all 14 DE genes fall within the overlapping deletion interval strengthens the conclusion that these are the most relevant genes for early cortical development.

results.result: The authors identified 93 differentially expressed genes outside the 16p11.2 deletion interval, including genes with known relevance to neurodevelopment and ASD (e.g., CNTNAP2, LHFPL3). These genes are involved in synaptic function, and their differential expression in NPCs precedes morphological abnormalities observed in more mature neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 and C108-C114 demonstrate that 16p11.2 deletion affects gene expression beyond the deleted region. The enrichment for ASD-associated genes and synaptic function genes is well-documented, and the connection to prior findings in mature neurons provides biological context.

results.result: The authors found that MAPK3 (encoding Erk1) is downregulated in deletion NPCs and interacts with several other DE genes, supporting prior work implicating the Erk1 MAPK pathway in 16p11.2 phenotypes. However, no changes in NPC proliferation were observed, suggesting MAPK3 may not influence proliferation at this developmental stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 appropriately connect the MAPK3 finding to prior research while acknowledging that proliferation effects were not observed at the NPC stage. The consistency with prior work (Deshpande et al., 2017) regarding lack of proliferation changes strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: The authors found reduced expression of KCTD13 and TAOK2 across all deletion lines and speculate that this may impact cortical network development and synaptic function based on prior functional studies of these genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by the expression data and prior functional studies. However, C118 is speculative as no functional experiments were performed in the current study to test whether reduced expression in NPCs actually impacts cortical network development or synaptic tone. This represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: The DE gene list includes genes involved in cell motility, cytoskeletal organization, glucose metabolism, and several microRNAs (including miR-6723, miR-301B, miR-637) with potential roles in proliferation and cellular function.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C127 appropriately characterize the functional categories of DE genes based on known gene functions and prior literature. The identification of miRNAs is notable, though the authors acknowledge their sequencing protocol was not optimized for mature miRNA detection.

results.result: Four deletion clones contained additional CNVs (14q11.1, 14q11.2, 7p11.2) potentially associated with neurodevelopmental abnormalities, but these did not significantly affect the average fold change of DE genes compared to other deletion clones.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131 appropriately document additional CNVs and analyze their potential impact. The finding that these additional CNVs do not significantly affect DE gene expression patterns supports the conclusion that the observed transcriptional changes are primarily due to the 16p11.2 deletion.

results.result: WGCNA identified 123 gene expression modules, with 20 showing significant associations with clinical variables. Fifteen modules correlated with clinical phenotypes, and four modules showed strong correlations with Age, Height Z-score, Weight Z-score, and Head Circumference Z-score. The modules did not contain genes distinguishing DEL from WT samples, and 16p11.2 genes were most frequently in the grey module.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 and C133-C137 present appropriate WGCNA analysis identifying gene modules associated with clinical traits. The finding that these modules are distinct from the DEL vs. WT comparison suggests patient-specific variation beyond the core deletion effect.

results.result: GSEA of genes in trait-associated modules identified 69 gene sets upregulated in high BMI individuals, with the majority involving metabolic processes but the strongest enrichments in signaling pathways and cellular responses to external stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 and C140-C141 present appropriate GSEA analysis of WGCNA modules. The finding that metabolic genes are most numerous but signaling pathways show strongest enrichment is clearly documented in the data.

results.result: The pink4 module showed high significance and correlation with multiple clinical phenotypes including Age, Weight Z-score (positive), Height Z-score (negative), Head Circumference Z-score (negative), and Language deficits. This module contains 45 genes including regulators of MAPK (FGF1) and Wnt (WIF1) signaling pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 identify the pink4 module as particularly relevant to 16p11.2 phenotypes. The correlations with multiple clinical traits are well-documented, though the interpretation that this reflects a common gene module linking previously unconnected features (C93) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: The authors conclude that cellular metabolism is a compelling avenue for investigation and that patient-specific transcriptional abnormalities may interact with core 16p11.2 deficiency to generate heterogeneous phenotypes. Some correlations involve genes outside the 16p11.2 deletion and are detected even in neural progenitors for traits like BMI.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C132, C138-C139, C142-C143, C147, and C152-C154 represent interpretations of the WGCNA findings. These are reasonable conclusions supported by the data, though they represent hypotheses about mechanisms rather than demonstrated causal relationships.

results.result: The authors found associations between Weight Z-score and insulin/IGF2 expression, and between the pink4 module and Head Circumference/Language traits. They speculate about potential mechanisms involving insulin signaling, MAPK pathways, NPC proliferation, and circuit assembly.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is supported by the WGCNA data. However, C146, C148-C150 are highly speculative interpretations that extend beyond the data. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('may', 'could', 'suggests', 'invites speculation'), but these represent hypotheses requiring future experimental validation rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: The authors emphasize the importance of screening for cryptic plasmid integration, provide a computational pipeline for detection, and present evidence that transcriptional effects are primarily due to reprogramming factor expression (particularly POU5F1) rather than insertional mutagenesis. One clone with silenced integration showed an expression profile similar to integration-free clones.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C166 provide important methodological insights and resources. The evidence that effects are due to factor expression rather than insertion (C159-C161) is supported by the silenced integration clone analysis. The computational pipeline (C165-C166) is a valuable contribution to the field.

results.result: The manuscript provides context about hiPSC technology, its limitations (intra/inter-patient variability, epigenetic memory), prior work on 16p11.2 hiPSCs, and identifies a gap in knowledge regarding gene expression in early neuroepithelial precursors.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24, C95, C97-C98 appropriately cite prior literature to establish context and justify the current study. These represent accurate summaries of the field and identify the specific gap addressed by this work.

results.result: The authors conclude that this collection of 65 hiPSC lines represents an important resource for studying 16p11.2 CNVs, with comprehensive quality control, screening for integration, and identification of early transcriptomic perturbations that may prime later functional alterations. The resource is publicly available through SFARI.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C167-C172 appropriately summarize the resource and its value. The comprehensive characterization, integration screening, and public availability make this a significant contribution to the field. The interpretation that early transcriptomic changes may act as 'priming events' (C168) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: The authors claim that transcriptomic profiling identified alterations in gene expression patterns that precede morphological abnormalities reported at later stages, with disruptions in gene programs related to nervous system function and cellular metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 are supported by the differential expression and WGCNA analyses. The connection to 'preceding' later morphological abnormalities is based on comparison to prior work (Deshpande et al., 2017) showing neuronal phenotypes, making this a reasonable temporal inference.

results.result: The authors generated 65 hiPSC clones from 13 donors with 16p11.2 CNVs (10 deletion, 3 duplication) using episomal reprogramming vectors. These clones were characterized for pluripotency, karyotype, and CNV status, and are available through SFARI as a resource for studying 16p11.2-related neurodevelopmental disorders.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as 'a valuable cellular resource' and state that 'the production of this large set of iPSC clones...make this paper, as a Tools and Resource publication, a valuable resource for the community.' The acceptance summary confirms this is 'an important resource paper' describing the iPSC collection.

results.result: Despite using non-integrating episomal reprogramming vectors, many hiPSC clones contained randomly integrated reprogramming vectors that led to inappropriate expression of reprogramming genes (particularly POU5F1/OCT3/4) in neural progenitor cells. This integration had a more penetrant impact on genome-wide gene expression (>3600 DE genes) than the 16p11.2 CNVs themselves, necessitating exclusion of integration-positive clones from subsequent analyses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as 'a cautionary tale about some unexpected consequences of the reprogramming process' and 'the cautionary tale concerning vector integration' is highlighted as a key contribution. The acceptance summary specifically mentions this provides 'a cautionary tale about some unexpected consequences of the reprogramming process.'

results.result: The authors developed a customizable bioinformatic pipeline using pseudo-alignment to detect and quantify expression from cryptically integrated reprogramming plasmids versus genomic sources. This computationally lightweight tool can be run on a laptop and is provided as a resource for other researchers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly critique this methodological development, and the acceptance summary notes the paper provides 'a plethora of information' including methodological contributions. The tool is presented as part of the quality control strategy that reviewers implicitly accept by approving the resource.

results.result: The authors successfully differentiated 40 hiPSC clones into cortical neural progenitor cells (NPCs) using dual-SMAD inhibition, demonstrating proper rosette formation, radial glial identity (PAX6+), epithelial polarity markers, and enrichment of anterior/dorsal cortical markers. No subjective differences in rosette formation were observed between WT and 16p11.2 CNV clones.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the differentiation protocol or characterization. They request additional information about controls and QC (point 5a-e) but do not question the basic differentiation results. The acceptance summary acknowledges 'changes in gene expression observed when neural progenitors are derived from these iPSCs.'

results.result: After excluding integration-positive clones, insufficient duplication clones remained (n=4) for meaningful analysis, so the study focused exclusively on deletion clones. Integration-free deletion and WT clones clustered by genotype in PCA after batch correction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly critique this limitation, stating 'Unless the authors wish to include data for the duplication clones, The title "16p11.2 CNV imparts…" should be "16p11.2 microdeletion imparts…"' (point 4). This indicates the exclusion of duplication data is a significant limitation that affects the scope of conclusions.

results.result: In integration-free NPCs, 14 genes within the 16p11.2 deletion interval showed significant downregulation (including MAZ, DOC2A, PRRT2, TAOK2, MAPK3, KCTD13, SEZ6L2), consistent with copy number-dependent effects. In total, 107 differentially expressed genes were identified (adjusted p<0.05), with the 14 16p11.2 genes among the most affected (≥1.5-fold change).
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'the transcriptional changes reported are quite limited' (point 3) and request reanalysis using linear mixed models to properly account for repeated measures from the same donors (point 2). They also request validation in existing datasets (point 6b) and note the lack of observable phenotypic differences (point 7), suggesting the transcriptional findings alone are insufficient.

results.result: Beyond the 16p11.2 interval, 93 additional genes were differentially expressed, including genes associated with ASD (e.g., CNTNAP2, LHFPL3) and genes relevant to excitatory synapses. An alternative linear mixed model analysis identified 40 DE genes, with 17 overlapping the primary analysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers request reanalysis using proper statistical methods for repeated measures (point 2), which was subsequently performed and showed only partial overlap (17/40 genes). They also request integration with existing datasets and validation (points 6a-c), indicating uncertainty about the robustness and biological significance of these findings.

results.result: Differentially expressed genes impinge on signaling pathways relevant to neurodevelopment, including MAPK/ERK signaling (MAPK3 downregulated), synaptic genes (KCTD13, TAOK2), and genes related to neurite branching and synapse development. However, no changes in NPC proliferation were observed despite MAPK3 downregulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note 'no data of any observable phenotype was presented' (point 3) and specifically ask 'Are the authors able to comment on any phenotypic differences that they did observe between microdeletion lines and wt lines?' (point 7). The lack of functional phenotypes despite transcriptional changes raises questions about biological significance.

results.result: WGCNA identified gene modules correlated with clinical phenotypes including BMI, language deficits, head circumference, and age. The pink4 module showed strong correlations with Weight Z-score and language traits, containing genes involved in MAPK and Wnt signaling. Metabolic and signaling pathway genes were enriched in modules associated with patient traits, suggesting links between cellular metabolism and neurodevelopmental outcomes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly comment on the WGCNA analysis, but their concerns about statistical methods (point 2), limited transcriptional changes (point 3), and lack of phenotypic validation (point 7) apply to these correlative findings. The request to 'tone down' conclusions and 'draw more conservative conclusions' (point 3) suggests skepticism about interpretations linking gene expression to clinical features.

results.result: Four of 13 integration-free deletion clones contained additional CNVs (14q11.1, 14q11.2, 7p11.2) potentially associated with neurodevelopmental abnormalities. However, there was no significant difference in average fold change of DE genes between clones with and without additional CNVs, suggesting these do not account for the transcriptional changes reported.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding or the authors' interpretation that additional CNVs are unlikely to confound results. The analysis addressing this potential confound strengthens the study's quality control, which reviewers generally support.

results.result: Differentially expressed genes include those related to cell motility and cytoskeletal organization (SELE, TEKT4, TUBGCP4, KLHL4), glucose metabolism (TLCD3B, FBP2, ALDOA), and several microRNAs including miR-6723 (most significantly changed) and miRNAs involved in proliferation (miR-301B, miR-637).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not specifically comment on these findings, but their general concern about 'quite limited' transcriptional changes (point 3) and lack of phenotypic validation (point 7) applies. These are presented as secondary observations without functional validation.

results.result: The pink4 module's association with head circumference suggests links to NPC proliferation abnormalities, while its correlation with language deficits may reflect effects on circuit assembly. The correlation between Weight Z-score and specific gene expression (e.g., INS) indicates these are not simply age-related changes.
results.evaluation: These are speculative interpretations that reviewers would likely view skeptically given their instruction to 'tone down' statements and 'draw more conservative conclusions' (point 3). The lack of functional validation and the correlative nature of these findings limit support for mechanistic claims.

results.result: The transcriptomic data identify early network perturbations in NPCs that may act as priming events for later functional alterations observed in more mature neurons, providing novel candidates for future studies of 16p11.2 deletion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state it is 'misleading to "strongly suggest" that "16p11.2 deletion may impact many functions important to neurodevelopment and neuropsychiatric disease"' given the limited transcriptional changes and lack of phenotypic data (point 3). This interpretation goes beyond what the data support according to reviewer standards.

Peer reviewers explicitly recognize this as 'a valuable cellular resource' for the community, confirming strong support for the resource claims.

Both address hiPSC quality control (C45-C52). OpenEval finds the pluripotency validation and characterization methods comprehensive and well-supported. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their overall approval of the resource, though they request additional QC information.

Perfect overlap on neural differentiation claims (C53-C61). OpenEval finds the characterization demonstrates successful differentiation with appropriate methods. Peer reviewers do not challenge the differentiation protocol but request additional control information, indicating general acceptance with minor clarifications needed.

Both address cryptic vector integration (C27-C29, C62-C73). OpenEval finds the evidence compelling and the exclusion of Int+ clones well-justified. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as 'a cautionary tale' and a key contribution, showing strong agreement on the importance and validity of these findings.

Peer reviewers would likely view skeptically given instruction to 'draw more conservative conclusions,' showing agreement on insufficient support for mechanistic claims.
